5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: H. A motion blur augmentation which selects sections of the image to apply a kernel to over a directional vector - mimicking the blur caused by animal movement

The train-test mismatch here is not photometry or colour, it is capture dynamics.

The deployment rig is fixed geometry, fixed illumination, fixed exposure. 7 m baseline, camera bolted to one rock face looking at the other, focused at the mid-point, ISO 190 f/4 1/500 s, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise under a fixed-brightness IR illuminator, one frame every 30 s. In deployment brightness is essentially constant and the scene is effectively monochrome IR. That means linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C, RGB swizzle I, colour noise J and black-white noise K are all injecting variation that will not exist at test time and will encourage reliance on colour cues that are absent in the field. Scale D is also largely locked by the 7 m standoff and the 50 mm optics, and a vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals.

The GBIF multimedia the model will be trained on is the opposite: daylight, visible colour, variable cameras, variable distances, and overwhelmingly curated static natural-history shots. The images are posed, sharp, and motion-free.

In the ravine the animals are not posed. The pinch point funnels movement, and the camera samples once every 30 s. The animal is almost always in transit when the shutter fires. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few metres per second through a narrow corridor will traverse a non-trivial fraction of its body width during the 2 ms exposure, and limbs and heads are routinely captured mid-stride. The result is spatially localised, directional smearing along the travel axis, with the rock background remaining essentially sharp. That motion signature is ubiquitous in deployment and essentially absent from GBIF.

A directional motion-blur augmentation applied to animal-sized regions replicates exactly that physics: it degrades high-frequency edge cues that an EfficientNet-B7 would otherwise over-rely on from the clean GBIF set, and forces the network to learn shape and texture invariants that survive small in-frame translation. An isotropic Gaussian blur G blurs the rocks and background as well as the animal and does not match the depth-dependent optical defocus that is claimed for this rig. The claimed DOF numbers depend on an unstated circle of confusion and sensor size, and the specification itself is contradictory, “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”. On the narrow ground plane of a pinch point the usable depth is a thin slab, so systematic defocus is a second-order effect compared with transit motion.

Horizontal flip F is physically plausible but the gain is limited: the rock faces are not symmetric and the corridor imposes a strong left-right travel prior. It does not address the motion-free vs motion-rich gap that separates curated GBIF stills from real camera-trap captures. Motion blur does.

Hence of the listed options the augmentation that closes the most realistic domain gap between static daylight GBIF training and moving night-IR camera-trap deployment is the directional motion blur.

The train/test mismatch here is not primarily photometric or a global optical defocus, it is a capture-dynamics mismatch.

The EfficientNet will be trained on several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species. Those are curated, daylight, mostly static natural-history photographs where the animal is posed, presented head-on and critically sharp. The deployment rig is a fixed night IR trap in a 7 m pinch point: camera bolted to the face of one rock, looking straight down the corridor to the other rock, fixed brightness IR illumination, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, one frame every 30 s from 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, focused at the mid-point ~3.5 m.

Illumination is essentially constant. The IR illuminator is fixed brightness and the exposure is locked, so global linear/non-linear brightness jitter A,B,C, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K and RGB swizzle I are modelling variation that does not exist at test time and in fact encourages reliance on colour/daylight cues that are absent under fixed IR.

Geometry is essentially fixed too. The 7 m baseline and the narrow pinch point lock nominal object scale and viewpoint. Scale augmentation D is therefore of little use and a vertical flip E is physically impossible for a terrestrial mammal. A horizontal flip F is plausible because an animal can transit left-to-right or right-to-left, but it is a second order data-multiplying trick compared with the dynamics of the capture.

That leaves the optical quality mismatch. The defocus argument for G assumes animals spend a large fraction of time well outside the ~3.0–4.2 m in-focus interval computed for a 50 mm f/4 lens focused at 3.5 m. In a rock-funnelled pinch point the animal’s body is forced to stay on, and within a metre of, the optical axis and close to the mid-depth plane. The depth of a mammal itself is only ~0.3–0.6 m, so the majority of a transit will actually lie inside or very near the depth of field. The claimed systematic defocus is therefore much smaller in practice than the idealised DOF calculation suggests, and a uniform 11×11 σ=3 isotropic Gaussian applied to the whole image is a poor proxy for the depth-dependent, radially symmetric defocus that would remain; it will also blur the rock faces that in the real rig stay relatively sharp relative to the animal and will destroy high frequency texture that the model needs for species discrimination.

What is consistently absent from GBIF and routinely present in the field is motion during the exposure. The camera fires every 30 s with no trigger, so the shutter at 1/500 s will almost always catch an animal mid-transit. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s through the corridor will move a non-trivial fraction of its body width and its limbs will be in motion during the 2 ms exposure. That produces a directional, object-localised smear along the travel axis, not an isotropic Gaussian. GBIF images never contain that signature.

A motion-blur augmentation that applies a directional kernel to animal-sized regions mimics the physically unavoidable streaking that will appear in deployment while leaving the static rock background sharp, exactly matching the generation process. It forces the EfficientNet to learn shape and texture cues that are invariant to small directional smearing, which is the realism gap that separates clean static GBIF portraits from real camera-trap transits. Gaussian defocus, scale jitter and photometric jitter are secondary or mismatched under fixed IR, fixed geometry and fixed exposure; motion is the dominant deployment effect that is missing from the training distribution.

Operating constraints that are now repeatedly agreed:
* Illumination / modality: fixed-brightness IR illuminator, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s. Deployment brightness is essentially constant and the scene is essentially monochrome IR, R≈G≈B. Linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C, colour noise J, black-white noise K and RGB swizzle I do not match test statistics; brightness jitter is variation that does not exist at test time.
* Geometry / scale: camera bolted to rock face looking 7 m down a pinch point, 50 mm focal length, focus at the 3.5 m mid-point. Apparent size and viewpoint are essentially fixed in the field. Scale augmentation D is largely irrelevant. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-right transit but background is not strictly symmetric and is a second-order gain.
* Modality gap is the dominant unaddressed shift: daylight RGB GBIF → fixed-brightness IR monochrome. No listed augmentation faithfully creates grayscale/IR statistics. RGB channel swizzle I is the closest listed proxy to colour-decorrelation, but it does not produce IR grayscale. A true fix would be grayscale/IR simulation and trap fine-tuning, which is not in the list, giving a strong None L argument.

The live disagreement is defocus vs motion.

Defocus / Gaussian blur G camp:
* f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m. Hyperfocal ≈ f²/Nc ≈20–31 m → near ≈ H s/(H+s) ~3.0 m, far ≈ H s/(H-s) ~4.2 m. DOF ≈ ~1 m in a 7 m deep channel.
* Systematic depth-of-field defocus is guaranteed by the fixed focus/aperture geometry and is present for most of the traverse. GBIF is essentially all sharp daylight colour. An isotropic Gaussian blur is the canonical proxy for that optical defocus.
* 1/500 s at ISO 190 gives low read/photon noise and a short motion integration time, so motion blur H is small and second order. Horizontal flip is plausible but second order relative to pervasive defocus. Colour/brightness/noise ops are mismatched to fixed IR.

Motion blur H camp:
* Train-test mismatch is dynamic, not photometric. GBIF multimedia is curated, static, daylight natural history. Deployment images are of animals in transit through a funnel sampled every 30 s.
* Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s will translate a non-trivial fraction of its body width during the ~2 ms exposure; limbs/head are mid-stride. The blur is directional, spatially localised to the animal, background rocks stay sharp.
* A directional, region-selective motion blur mimics that physical generation process and forces the network to rely on shape/texture invariants rather than high-frequency edge cues. Defocus G is argued to be overestimated: animals are constrained to the pinch plane near the mid-depth, animal depth is ~0.3–0.6 m, and the quoted DOF numbers are sensitive to an unstated CoC and to the contradictory lens spec “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”. A uniform 11×11 σ=3 Gaussian also blurs the static rock background unrealistically.

Other notes from round 1:
* Several colleagues explicitly state the colour → IR modality shift is the real failure mode and none of A–K closes it; RGB swizzle I is at best a weak colour-invariance proxy.
* Scale D is essentially fixed by the 7 m standoff and fixed optics.
* The 11×11 σ=3 Gaussian is not a noise augmentation but a defocus proxy.
* Horizontal flip F is widely accepted as the only safe geometric invariance, but most treat it as second order to the optical / motion effect.

Unresolved tension: relative weight of guaranteed depth-of-field defocus vs directional motion smear. Defocus is a guaranteed optics effect independent of speed; motion is speed-dependent but is ubiquitous because the trap samples a funnel with no trigger. Modality shift remains the largest perceptual difference but is unaddressed by any listed transform.

Current best working hypothesis: among the strictly listed options the physically grounded effect that is guaranteed by the stated focus/f-number/geometry and is missing from curated GBIF is systematic defocus, best approximated by Gaussian blur G. Horizontal flip F is the only plausible geometric invariance. Motion blur H is a credible alternative, with strong arguments that the 1/500 s exposure and pinch-plane constraint make directional smear the dominant train-test visual difference and that a global isotropic Gaussian is a poor physical proxy. The ideal fix remains grayscale/IR simulation and trap fine-tuning, which is not present in the list, supporting the None L strict interpretation.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deployment set is not the GBIF set and the domain shift is multi-factorial and largely unaddressed by the listed ops.

* Photometry / modality. Deployment is night only, 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness IR illuminator, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s. Brightness and colour statistics are essentially constant in the field and the images are effectively monochrome IR, R≈G≈B. Training is daylight colour GBIF media with highly variable white balance, exposure and backgrounds. Linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K and RGB channel swizzle I do not simulate IR/grey and in fact encourage reliance on colour cues that are absent at test time. Brightness jitter is actively mismatched to a fixed illumination rig. The dominant colour/day → IR/monochrome modality shift is not closed by any of A–K; a true fix would be grayscale/IR simulation and trap fine-tuning. Colleague 4/10/12 note that in the strict sense none of the listed augmentations fully bridges this gap, so L is defensible.

* Geometry / scale. The rig is fixed to a rock face, 7 m to the opposite rock, looking down a pinch point, optics fixed, focused at the mid-point ~3.5 m. Apparent object scale and background are quasi-constant. Scale augmentation D is therefore unhelpful. A vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. A horizontal flip F is physically plausible – animals can transit the pinch point left-to-right or right-to-left – and is the only geometric augmentation that stays inside the deployment physics. It is a modest left-right invariance gain, not a domain-mismatch corrector. Several colleagues rate F as the safest geometric invariance.

* Optics. f≈50 mm, N=4.0, focus s≈3.5 m gives hyperfocal ≈ f²/Nc ≈ 20-31 m for a normal CoC and a DOF ≈ ~3.0–4.2 m, i.e. ~0.8–1.2 m in focus within a 7 m channel. Animals are therefore systematically defocused when they are not at the exact mid-plane. That is a guaranteed, deployment-constant imaging effect absent from curated GBIF images. A moderate isotropic Gaussian blur like G is the standard proxy for that depth-of-field defocus. The 11×11 σ≈3 px blur is argued by colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 as the most deployment-relevant optical regulariser. The lens spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”; DOF numbers are CoC sensitive and the background rocks will also be defocused, which a global Gaussian mimics but is criticised by the motion camp as blurring static cues that remain sharp in the field.

* Motion. 1/500 s at ISO 190 is fast and low noise. Even at a few m/s the in-exposure translation is a few cm, a few pixels on the sensor. Motion blur H is therefore argued by colleagues 1,13,14,7,5,9 as the key capture-dynamics gap: GBIF is static posed daylight, the trap samples a funnelled transit once every 30 s, so animals are routinely mid-stride at shutter. A directional, region-selective motion blur mimics a small streak on the animal while the rocks stay sharp, forcing shape/texture invariance. The defocus camp counters that 1/500 s freezes in-plane motion to a second-order effect and that the systematic DOF defocus affects essentially every capture outside the narrow focus slice, whereas motion is speed dependent and mostly axial.

Unresolved tension persists. The biggest true domain gap is colour/daylight GBIF → fixed IR monochrome night. None of A–K removes colour or simulates IR reflectance; channel permutation I only decorrelates colour. Brightness jitter is mismatched to fixed illumination. Among the physically plausible options that do not inject unnatural variation, horizontal flip F is the safest geometric invariance and Gaussian defocus blur G is the only optical effect guaranteed by the stated focus/f-number geometry. Motion blur H is repeatedly argued as the main “real vs curated” difference but its magnitude is limited by the 1/500 s shutter and the mostly axial transit. Current belief remains that of the listed operations G is the most deployment-relevant regulariser for the guaranteed optical mismatch, with F as a useful second-order invariance, while acknowledging the dominant colour→IR shift remains unmitigated by any listed augmentation and the motion-vs-defocus debate is still open.

reflection_text.4:
The deployment rig is a highly constrained night-IR trap: camera bolted to a rock face 7 m down a pinch point, 50 mm effective focal length at f/4.0, ISO 190, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illumination, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, one frame every 30 s, focused at ~3.5 m mid-point. Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species, i.e. daylight, visible colour, variable camera pose/distance, largely static, sharp exemplars. 17 species.

Domain gaps therefore are:
* modality / photometry: deployment is essentially monochrome R≈G≈B under fixed illumination and locked exposure. Global brightness is essentially constant. Linear/non-linear brightness A,B,C, RGB swizzle I, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K are all mismatched to test statistics and encourage reliance on colour/daylight cues absent at test time.
* geometry / scale: 7 m standoff and narrow pinch point lock nominal object scale and viewpoint. Scale D is essentially irrelevant. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-right transit and is a safe geometric invariance but second order compared with image-quality effects.
* optics: f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m → hyperfocal ≈ f²/Nc ≈20-31 m, near≈ H s/(H+s)≈3.0 m, far≈ H s/(H-s)≈4.2 m, i.e. ~0.8-1.2 m DOF in a 7 m channel. Depth-of-field defocus is therefore a systematic, deployment-constant degradation for animals off the focus plane and is essentially absent from sharp GBIF media. 
* dynamics: animals are funnelled through the corridor and the camera fires every 30 s with no trigger. Motion during the 2 ms exposure, gait phase and transit direction create a small, spatially localised, directional smear on the animal while rock background stays sharp. GBIF is curated static natural-history photography.

Colleague split:
Defocus camp 2,3,6,8,10,11,12,4 argues the guaranteed hardware effect is defocus. 1/500 s freezes in-plane translation enough that motion blur H is small/secondary, and an isotropic Gaussian blur G is the canonical proxy for depth-of-field blur. Horizontal mirroring F is plausible but secondary. The colour→IR shift is not closed by any listed op; ideal fix would be grayscale/IR simulation / fine-tuning, so strictly L would be correct.

Motion camp 1,5,7,13,14 argues the train-test gap is capture dynamics not photometry. Brightness/scale/blur are locked, the real gap is static sharp GBIF vs moving night-IR transit. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s can smear a non-trivial fraction of body width/limb during exposure, directional and object-localised. A directional motion-blur kernel on animal regions mimics this; isotropic Gaussian G blurs rocks and background unphysically and overestimates defocus for animals constrained near the optical axis.

Additional notes:
* RGB channel swizzle I is the closest listed proxy for colour invariance, but it does not produce monochrome IR statistics. Brightness jitter A,B,C is counter-productive with fixed IR.
* Lens spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”, CoC unspecified, so DOF numbers are sensitive.
* Unresolved: magnitude of in-exposure translation vs depth-dependent defocus for animals confined to a pinch point slab; whether isotropic Gaussian is an adequate proxy for defocus vs a local directional motion blur.
* Persistent belief: photometric augmentations are irrelevant, vertical flip harmful, scale irrelevant. The dominant unaddressed modality shift is colour/day → IR/monochrome, not present in A-K. Among listed ops the physically guaranteed simulable effect is depth-of-field defocus G, with H as a strong alternative interpretation of the dynamics gap, and F as the only safe geometric invariance.

The deployment set is not the GBIF set and the domain shift is multi-factorial and largely unaddressed by the listed ops.

* Photometry / modality. Deployment is night only, 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness IR illuminator, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s. Brightness and colour statistics are essentially constant in the field and the images are effectively monochrome IR, R≈G≈B. Training is daylight colour GBIF media with highly variable white balance, exposure and backgrounds. Linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K and RGB channel swizzle I do not simulate IR/grey and in fact encourage reliance on colour cues that are absent at test time. Brightness jitter is actively mismatched to a fixed illumination rig. The dominant colour/day → IR/monochrome modality shift is not closed by any of A–K; a true fix would be grayscale/IR simulation and trap fine-tuning. Colleague 4/10/12 note that in the strict sense none of the listed augmentations fully bridges this gap, so L is defensible.

* Geometry / scale. The rig is fixed to a rock face, 7 m to the opposite rock, looking down a pinch point, optics fixed, focused at the mid-point ~3.5 m. Apparent object scale and background are quasi-constant. Scale augmentation D is therefore unhelpful. A vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. A horizontal flip F is physically plausible – animals can transit the pinch point left-to-right or right-to-left – and is the only geometric augmentation that stays inside the deployment physics. It is a modest left-right invariance gain, not a domain-mismatch corrector. Several colleagues rate F as the safest geometric invariance.

* Optics. f≈50 mm, N=4.0, focus s≈3.5 m gives hyperfocal ≈ f²/Nc ≈ 20-31 m for a normal CoC and a DOF ≈ ~3.0–4.2 m, i.e. ~0.8–1.2 m in focus within a 7 m channel. Animals are therefore systematically defocused when they are not at the exact mid-plane. That is a guaranteed, deployment-constant imaging effect absent from curated GBIF images. A moderate isotropic Gaussian blur like G is the standard proxy for that depth-of-field defocus. The 11×11 σ≈3 px blur is argued by colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 as the most deployment-relevant optical regulariser. The lens spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”; DOF numbers are CoC sensitive and the background rocks will also be defocused, which a global Gaussian mimics but is criticised by the motion camp as blurring static cues that remain sharp in the field.

* Motion. 1/500 s at ISO 190 is fast and low noise. Even at a few m/s the in-exposure translation is a few cm, a few pixels on the sensor. Motion blur H is therefore argued by colleagues 1,13,14,7,5,9 as the key capture-dynamics gap: GBIF is static posed daylight, the trap samples a funnelled transit once every 30 s, so animals are routinely mid-stride at shutter. A directional, region-selective motion blur mimics a small streak on the animal while the rocks stay sharp, forcing shape/texture invariance. The defocus camp counters that 1/500 s freezes in-plane motion to a second-order effect and that the systematic DOF defocus affects essentially every capture outside the narrow focus slice, whereas motion is speed dependent and mostly axial.

Unresolved tension persists. The biggest true domain gap is colour/daylight GBIF → fixed IR monochrome night. None of A–K removes colour or simulates IR reflectance; channel permutation I only decorrelates colour. Brightness jitter is mismatched to fixed illumination. Among the physically plausible options that do not inject unnatural variation, horizontal flip F is the safest geometric invariance and Gaussian defocus blur G is the only optical effect guaranteed by the stated focus/f-number geometry. Motion blur H is repeatedly argued as the main “real vs curated” difference but its magnitude is limited by the 1/500 s shutter and the mostly axial transit. Current belief remains that of the listed operations G is the most deployment-relevant regulariser for the guaranteed optical mismatch, with F as a useful second-order invariance, while acknowledging the dominant colour→IR shift remains unmitigated by any listed augmentation and the motion-vs-defocus debate is still open.

* Geometry/scale locked: camera bolted rock face to rock face 7 m apart, 50 mm focal length, focus at ~3.5 m mid-point. Apparent size/viewpoint quasi-constant. Scale D irrelevant. Vertical flip E physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-right transit, widely accepted as the only safe geometric invariance, but treated as second order.
* Modality gap is dominant unaddressed shift: daylight RGB GBIF → fixed-brightness IR monochrome. No listed augmentation faithfully creates grayscale/IR statistics. RGB swizzle I is the closest listed proxy to colour-decorrelation but does not produce IR grayscale. Ideal fix would be grayscale/IR simulation + trap fine-tuning, supporting a strict None L argument.

Live disagreement is defocus vs motion.

Defocus / Gaussian blur G camp:
* f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m. Hyperfocal ≈ f²/Nc ≈20–31 m → near ≈3.0 m, far≈4.0–4.2 m. DOF ≈~1 m in a 7 m channel.
* Systematic depth-of-field defocus is guaranteed by fixed focus/aperture geometry and is present for most of the traverse. GBIF is essentially all sharp daylight colour. Isotropic Gaussian blur is canonical proxy for that optical defocus.
* 1/500 s =2 ms at ISO 190 gives low noise and short integration; in-plane motion blur is small and speed dependent. Horizontal flip is plausible but second order relative to pervasive defocus. Colour/brightness/noise ops mismatched to fixed IR.

Motion blur H camp:
* Train-test mismatch is dynamic, not photometric. GBIF multimedia is curated static daylight natural history. Deployment fires every 30 s with no trigger in a funnel; animals are transiting when shutter opens.
* Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of body width during ~2 ms exposure; gait cycle gives different phases within frame. Blur is directional, spatially localised to animal, rock background stays sharp.
* Gaussian G is argued to be overestimated: DOF numbers are sensitive to unstated CoC/sensor and to contradictory lens spec “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”. Defocus is depth-varying/radial, not a uniform 11×11 σ=3 blur applied globally; a uniform Gaussian unrealistically blurs static rock faces that remain usable for localisation. Pinch geometry constrains animals to the optical axis and within ~0.3–0.6 m body depth, so residence time outside nominal focus slab is limited.
* Region-selective directional motion blur mimics physical generation and forces network to rely on shape/texture invariants rather than high-frequency edge cues present in GBIF.

Other persistent notes:
* Several colleagues explicitly state colour→IR modality shift is real failure mode and none A–K closes it.
* Scale D essentially fixed by 7 m standoff and fixed optics.
* 11×11 σ=3 Gaussian is defocus proxy, not noise.
* Horizontal flip F is widely accepted as only physically safe geometric augmentation, but second order.
* Unresolved tension: weight of guaranteed depth-of-field defocus independent of speed vs directional motion smear ubiquitous in funnel transit. Modality shift remains largest perceptual difference but unaddressed by list.

Current best working hypothesis remains split: among strictly listed options the physically grounded effect guaranteed by stated focus/f-number/geometry is systematic defocus, best approximated by Gaussian blur G; motion blur H is a credible alternative with strong arguments about background sharpness, spec contradiction, and dominance of transit dynamics over depth variation. The real unaddressed failure is daylight RGB → fixed IR monochrome, unclosed by any listed op.
Among simulable degradations, the core disagreement is systematic depth-of-field defocus vs in-exposure transit motion.
The uniform Gaussian G argument rests on a guaranteed depth-of-field loss for most of the 7 m corridor; the motion H argument rests on physical fidelity – region-selective directional smear with a sharp static background, and the critique that a global isotropic Gaussian mis-models both depth-varying defocus and the sharp rock reference.

Unresolved: exact CoC/sensor size, true DOF extent, actual animal speed distribution in the pinch point, and whether defocus or motion dominates the loss of high-frequency cues in practise.

reflection_text.6:
The train-test gap is hardware-imposed: GBIF daylight RGB free-form stills vs a fixed rig night IR trap.

Photometry / modality is locked in deployment. Fixed-brightness IR illuminator, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s. Deployment brightness is essentially constant and R≈G≈B. Linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K and RGB channel swizzle I therefore inject variation that will not exist at test time and encourage reliance on daylight colour cues absent under IR. The dominant modality shift day colour → fixed IR monochrome is not bridged by any listed op; in a strict sense L is true. I is the closest colour-agnostic proxy but does not create monochrome IR statistics.

Geometry / scale is locked. Camera bolted 7 m down a pinch point, f≈50 mm, focus at ~3.5 m mid-point. Apparent size and viewpoint are quasi-constant. Scale D is of little value. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-right transit through the pinch point and is a safe second-order geometric invariance, though rock background is not perfectly symmetric.

Optics. f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m → hyperfocal H≈f²/Nc≈20–31 m for normal CoC, near≈H s/(H+s)≈3.0 m, far≈H s/(H-s)≈4.0–4.2 m, i.e. ~1 m DOF in a 7 m corridor. Animals off the mid-plane are systematically defocused in every field frame. GBIF training is essentially all sharp. Gaussian blur G with 11×11 σ=3 is the canonical proxy for that depth-of-field defocus. Criticism in round 2: the spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”, DOF numbers depend on unstated CoC/sensor, defocus is depth-varying/radial not a uniform whole-image blur, and a global Gaussian blurs the rock background that in reality stays relatively sharp. Proponents of G argue defocus is guaranteed for the majority of transit and independent of speed, while motion is second order at 1/500 s =2 ms, and isotropic Gaussian is the standard simulable regulariser.

Motion vs defocus remains the core disagreement. H supporters 1,13,14,5,7,9 argue the real dynamic gap is capture dynamics: camera fires every 30 s with no trigger in a funnel, animals are transiting mid-stride when shutter opens, 2 ms exposure still yields small directional, animal-localised smearing while rocks stay sharp, GBIF is curated static. Region-selective directional motion blur mimics that generation process and leaves background sharp. They argue DOF calculation is fragile, pinch constrains depth to ~0.3-0.6 m body depth and residence time near focus plane is high, and a uniform Gaussian unrealistically blurs static reference features.

G supporters 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 argue 1/500 s freezes lateral translation for mostly axial transit, motion blur is animal-speed dependent and second order, whereas defocus is present for essentially every capture outside the ~3.0-4.2 m slice and is hardware-constant. They accept the colour/IR gap is unclosed, but of the listed ops defocus simulation is the most deployment-relevant regulariser, with F as the only safe geometric invariance.

Overall ranking unchanged: the unaddressed failure mode is colour/day → IR/grey. Of the listed operations, the only physically guaranteed imaging effect that can be simulated is systematic defocus → G, with F as a cheap safe invariance and I as the best colour-agnostic proxy. H is a plausible alternative view with strong support arguing defocus is modest for animals constrained to the pinch plane and that capture dynamics, not optics, separates curated GBIF stills from live transit captures. Debate between G vs H remains unresolved; current round keeps numerical lead with G but critiques of uniform isotropic blur blurring background rocks are persistent.
reflection_text.2:
The deployment rig is fixed geometry / fixed photometry night IR. Camera at one rock face looking 7 m to the other, focused ~3.5 m mid-point, ~50 mm effective focal length, f/4.0, ISO 190, 1/500 s, one frame/30 s 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise under fixed-brightness IR illuminator. Mammals IR-blind, imaging is essentially monochrome IR, R≈G≈B, brightness essentially constant. Training is EfficientNet-B7 on several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species for 17 species. GBIF is curated daylight visible-RGB, variable camera pose/distance/lighting, sharp static subjects.

Domain gaps repeatedly flagged:
* Modality / colour: daylight colour RGB → fixed-brightness IR/grey. Photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K and RGB swizzle do not produce IR monochrome; they either inject variation absent at test time or at best force colour decorrelation. Colleagues 10,4,8,2 note this is the dominant shift and none of the listed ops faithfully simulates it. Colleague 10 argues channel swizzle I is the closest proxy for colour invariance; Colleague 4 argues even that is marginal and none of A-K materially improves.
* Geometry / scale: 7 m standoff and fixed optics make apparent scale and viewpoint quasi-constant. Scale D is low value. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible because animals can transit left-to-right or right-to-left; colleagues 12,3,5,8 argue this is the only geometrically valid invariance among the list; colleagues 11,2 argue background asymmetry makes gain second order.
* Optical defocus: f≈50 mm, N=4, focus ~3.5 m → hyperfocal ~20-31 m for normal CoC, DOF ~≈3.0-4.2 m, ~1 m around focus. Anything outside that slice in the 7 m ravine is systematically defocused. Colleagues 11,2,6,8,10,12 argue this is the guaranteed physical mismatch with sharp GBIF images and a moderate isotropic Gaussian blur G ~11×11 σ=3 px is the faithful simulation of that defocus. Colleague 1 argues the DOF numbers are sensitive to CoC and to the contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length” spec, and that a uniform Gaussian blurs the rock background which stays relatively sharp in the field.
* Motion: 1/500 s is fast. Pro-motion-blur colleagues 1,13,7,5,9,14 claim transit through narrow pinch point still yields directional smear and GBIF images are motion-free, so directional motion-blur H closes the realism gap and background stays sharp. Anti-motion colleagues 11,2,6,10 argue 1/500 s freezes motion for typical mammal speeds; defocus dominates.
* Brightness: deployment brightness is essentially constant under fixed IR illuminator; linear / non-linear brightness jitter A,B,C injects variation absent at test time. Colleague 14 argues luminance invariance B helps because training brightness is variable, but others say brightness is fixed at deployment so jitter is harmful.

Round 2 public re-statements reinforce the split:
G camp: 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8. Emphasis on guaranteed DOF defocus as hardware-imposed image quality loss absent from GBIF, motion frozen by 1/500 s, photometric augmentations mismatched to fixed IR, horizontal flip second order, colour/IR shift unaddressed by any listed op.
H camp: 1,13,14,5,7,9. Emphasis on capture dynamics gap: GBIF static posed vs field transit mid-stride; directional region-selective motion blur matches physics of moving animal with sharp rocks; Gaussian blur is isotropic and blurs background unrealistically; defocus is modest because animals stay near focus plane and depth is constrained by pinch.
F/colour proxy camp: horizontal flip as only safe geometric invariance; RGB swizzle I as closest colour-invariance proxy for IR shift.

Consensus points:
- Brightness / colour / noise ops A,B,C,I,J,K are mismatched to fixed IR illumination and may encourage reliance on colour cues absent at test.
- Vertical flip is implausible.
- Scale is essentially fixed.
- True needed adaptation is grayscale/IR simulation + depth-of-field defocus, none of which is exactly present.
- Among listed ops, Gaussian defocus G is physically guaranteed by focus/f-number geometry; horizontal mirroring F is the only geometrically plausible data multiplier; RGB swizzle I is the closest colour-invariance proxy; motion blur H is plausible only if in-exposure motion is non-negligible.

Unresolved: whether defocus blur or colour/IR invariance dominates deployment error; whether motion blur at 1/500 s is meaningful given the spec contradiction and directional transit; whether horizontal flip actually adds value given non-symmetric rock background. Strongest “none is sufficient” argument remains from colleagues 4 and 10: colour/day → monochrome/IR night shift is not addressed by any listed augmentation, so strictly none will materially improve deployment accuracy, and any improvement from G/H/F will be marginal relative to modality mismatch.

Earlier round concerns remain: fixed brightness makes A,B,C harmful; fixed geometry makes D,E largely irrelevant; IR monochrome means colour augmentations are not faithful; EfficientNet will over-rely on high-frequency edge cues from sharp GBIF data.
reflection_text.11:
The deployment is a night fixed-geometry IR trap vs GBIF daylight colour training.

Modality / photometry is locked in deployment: fixed-brightness IR illuminator, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, one frame every 30 s. Images are effectively monochrome R≈G≈B and global brightness is essentially constant. Hence linear / non-linear RGB/luminance brightness A,B,C, RGB swizzle I, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K inject variation never seen at test time and encourage reliance on daylight colour cues absent under IR. No listed operation closes the daylight RGB → fixed IR monochrome shift; ideal fix would be grayscale/IR simulation + trap fine-tuning, i.e. L is strictly defensible.

Geometry / scale is locked: camera bolted 7 m across the pinch point, ~50 mm optics, focus at ~3.5 m mid-point. Apparent size and viewpoint are quasi-constant, so scale D is of little value. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-right transit and is a safe second-order geometric invariance, but it does not address image quality.

The core disagreement is which simulable imaging degradation matters most.

Defocus camp: f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m → H≈f²/Nc≈20–31 m, near≈Hs/(H+s)≈3.0 m, far≈Hs/(H-s)≈4.0–4.2 m, ~1 m acceptable focus in a 7 m channel. GBIF is essentially all sharp daylight. Depth-of-field defocus is guaranteed by the stated focus/aperture geometry and is deployment-constant, absent from training. An 11×11 σ≈3 isotropic Gaussian is taken as the canonical proxy. Motion at 1/500 s =2 ms is claimed to freeze in-plane translation to a few pixels, so directional motion blur H is second order.

Motion camp: the spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length” and DOF depends sensitively on unstated CoC/sensor size. Defocus is depth-varying and radial, not a uniform global Gaussian; a global Gaussian unrealistically blurs the static rock faces and background that remain sharp in the field. The pinch point constrains depth and lateral position, residency outside the ~3.0–4.2 m slice is short. The real train-test gap is capture dynamics: GBIF is curated static daylight natural history, the trap fires every 30 s with no trigger in a funnel. Animals are transiting when the shutter opens. Even at 1/500 s a mammal at a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of body width during exposure, with limbs/torso at different gait phases. That yields spatially localised, directional smearing along the travel axis while the rock background stays crisp. A region-selective directional motion blur mimics that generation process and forces invariance to small streaks rather than over-reliance on pristine high-frequency edges. Horizontal flip F is acknowledged as plausible but secondary.

Shared points: brightness/tone/colour/noise/scale augmentations are mismatched to fixed IR, fixed range, fixed exposure. Vertical flip is impossible. Colour/IR modality gap is unclosed by any listed op. Consensus is G and H both improve over photometric augmentations, with F as safe geometric invariance.

Unresolved: exact DOF magnitude given contradictory lens spec and unknown CoC/sensor; whether systematic defocus dominates the whole 7 m channel in practice or whether constrained depth and mid-plane focus make defocus modest; whether 1/500 s truly freezes motion for typical mammals in a funnel. Under the restricted list the two physically grounded candidates remain defocus-simulating Gaussian G and region-selective directional motion blur H, with H gaining physical fidelity from background-preserving, spatially localised blur and from the explicit transit dynamics, while G gains from the guaranteed optical degradation math. L remains the strict ideal because the colour→IR shift is not closed.

Current belief remains split between guaranteed optical defocus G and capture-dynamics motion H, with strong arguments that a uniform Gaussian blurs background rocks that should stay sharp, and that lens spec ambiguity weakens the DOF calculation.
reflection_text.3:
The train-test gap is fixed IR camera-trap rig vs broad GBIF colour daylight scrape, not generic ImageNet.

Deployment physics that are stable:
* Fixed photometry/modality: rock face to rock face 7 m, 50 mm optics, f/4.0, ISO 190, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illumination, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, one frame every 30 s. Brightness/exposure essentially constant and R≈G≈B under IR.
* Scale/viewpoint essentially locked by 7 m pinch point and 50 mm optics.
* Focus at mid-point ~3.5 m. With f≈50 mm, N=4.0 hyperfocal H≈f²/Nc≈20–31 m → near≈3.0–3.2 m, far≈4.0–4.2 m, i.e. ~0.8–1.2 m of acceptable focus in a 7 m deep channel. The 7 m ravine is systematically out of focus except for brief transit through the focus plane. That is a deterministic optical degradation absent from GBIF.
* 1/500 s =2 ms, ISO 190 gives low noise. In-exposure translation is cm-scale for typical mammals, a few pixels at most, so motion smear is small and animal-speed dependent.
* Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically realisable left-to-right vs right-to-left transit and is a second-order data multiplier.

Training distribution:
Several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species, daylight, colour, heterogeneous cameras/distances/poses, essentially sharp and motion-free. EfficientNet-B7 ImageNet-initialised will learn colour and high-frequency edge cues abundant in GBIF but absent/different in field.

Implications for listed ops:
* Photometric ops A,B,C, colour noise J, RGB swizzle I, salt-and-pepper K: deployment brightness is constant and effectively monochrome IR. Global brightness/tone jitter injects variation that does not exist at test time and does not bridge daylight colour → IR/grey modality shift. Swizzle is closest proxy for colour invariance but does not produce required monochrome IR statistics.
* Scale D is fixed by rig.
* Horizontal flip F is plausible but smaller than image-quality mismatch. Vertical flip E harmful.
* Motion blur H camp: GBIF is static, field captures are of transiting animals; even at 1/500 s limbs/gait can produce small directional streaks localised to animal while rock background stays sharp. Directional region-selective blur forces shape invariance to capture dynamic. Counter: 1/500 s freezes translation to few cm, motion is speed dependent and smaller than guaranteed depth-of-field defocus; isotropic Gaussian G blurs background rocks unrealistically if applied globally, and defocus is depth-varying not uniform.
* Gaussian blur G camp: depth-of-field defocus from fixed focus at 3.5 m f/4 in 7 m channel is guaranteed and systematic; GBIF is essentially all sharp. 11×11 σ≈3 px isotropic Gaussian is canonical proxy for that optical degradation and forces features stable under blur that will affect most field captures. Counter: lens spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”; DOF numbers depend sensitively on CoC/sensor; corridor funnels animals close to focus plane; uniform Gaussian blurs static rock background that in reality stays relatively sharp; real defocus is depth-varying radial.

Unresolved dominant gap:
Largest real domain shift is modality: daylight RGB GBIF → fixed-brightness IR monochrome night. None of A-K faithfully simulates grayscale/IR reflectance or fixed illumination statistics. Ideal augmentation is not present – grayscale/IR simulation and fine-tuning on trap data – which is why several colleagues argue L, none of the above.

Current belief under restricted list:
The guaranteed deployment-constant image-quality mismatch that can be simulated with given ops is depth-of-field defocus, best approximated by Gaussian blur G. Horizontal mirroring F is only safe geometric invariance and a useful second-order regulariser. Motion blur H is plausible dynamic mismatch but with 1/500 s expected in-exposure smear is small and depth-of-field defocus is more systematic and larger on average, though region-selective motion blur correctly preserves sharp background whereas global Gaussian does not. Photometric augmentations, scale, vertical flip and generic noise are mismatched or harmful.

The true colour/day → IR/night shift remains unaddressed by any listed augmentation; if strict fidelity is required the correct answer is that none of the listed ops properly closes the gap. Of the listed candidates, G is the plurality, physically grounded regulariser that most closely mimics a deployment-guaranteed imaging effect absent from training, with F as secondary and H as a strong alternative view emphasizing capture dynamics over defocus.
reflection_text.9:

reflection_text.10:
The deployment distribution is fixed-geometry, fixed-photometry night IR vs a heterogeneous daylight colour GBIF training set. That locks test statistics and makes most ImageNet-style augmentations mismatched.

Photometry / modality lock:
* Fixed-brightness IR illuminator, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise → global brightness essentially constant, R≈G≈B in deployment. Linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K and RGB channel swizzle I therefore inject variation that will not exist at test time. Colleagues 10,4,12 note the dominant colour/day → IR/greyscale domain shift is not bridged by any listed op; I is at best a colour-invariance proxy.
* The true dominant failure remains daylight colour → fixed IR monochrome. None of A-K closes it; ideally grayscale/IR simulation + trap fine-tuning would be needed, i.e. L is the strictly correct statement. That is acknowledged by 10,11,12,4,6,8.

Geometry / scale lock:
* Camera bolted 7 m down a pinch point, 50 mm effective focal length, focus at ~3.5 m mid-plane. Apparent size is quasi-constant, so scale D is of little value. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-to-right vs right-to-left transit and is the only safe geometric invariance; colleagues 12,3,5,8 argue F is the only guaranteed geometric gain, but it is second order vs optical/dynamic degradation.

Optics vs motion tension:
* DOF camp: f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m → hyperfocal ≈ f²/Nc ≈20–31 m for a normal CoC. near≈Hs/(H+s)≈3.0 m, far≈Hs/(H-s)≈4.0–4.2 m → ~1 m of acceptable focus in a 7 m corridor. GBIF set is essentially all sharp daylight colour. An isotropic Gaussian defocus is the canonical proxy for systematic depth-of-field blur. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,6,8 argue G is the most deployment-relevant regulariser that can be simulated from the list.
* Critiques of G in round 2: the lens spec “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length” is contradictory; DOF numbers are CoC/sensor-sensitive; defocus is depth-varying and radial, not a uniform 11×11 σ=3 blur applied to the whole frame. A uniform Gaussian blurs the rock faces and background texture that in deployment remain a sharp, stable reference for localisation, and it blurs background and foreground identically, which is not how a fixed-focus lens behaves. Colleagues 1,13,7,14,5 point this out.
* Motion camp: 1/500 s =2 ms. Animals are transiting the corridor when the shutter fires, sampled every 30 s with no trigger. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of a body width during exposure and limbs/head/torso are at different gait phases in the same frame. That produces spatially localised, directional smearing along the travel axis while the static rocks stay crisp. A directional, region-selective motion blur replicates that generation process and forces EfficientNet-B7 to keep shape/texture cues that survive a small streak, rather than over-relying on pristine high-frequency edges in GBIF. Colleagues 1,13,7,14,5,9 argue H is the dominant domain gap; the pinch point constrains depth variation and residence time in extreme near/far zones is short relative to transit.
* Motion camp also notes the DOF argument is fragile: defocus is depth-varying, the pinch geometry constrains animals close to the optical axis and mid-plane, and the stated DOF hinges on unstated CoC/sensor. Defocus affects background rocks too, whereas the field rig keeps background relatively stable.

Current synthesis:
Colour/brightness/noise/scale/vertical flip augmentations are mismatched to fixed IR, fixed exposure, fixed-range rig. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible but a second-order gain.
The real unaddressed failure is daylight RGB → fixed IR monochrome, unclosed by any listed op.
Among simulable degradations, the core disagreement is systematic depth-of-field defocus vs in-exposure transit motion.
The uniform Gaussian G argument rests on a guaranteed depth-of-field loss for most of the 7 m corridor; the motion H argument rests on physical fidelity – region-selective directional smear with a sharp static background, and the critique that a global isotropic Gaussian mis-models both depth-varying defocus and the sharp rock reference.
Given the repeated critique of global isotropic blur blurring the static reference background and the contradictory lens spec / CoC sensitivity, the motion blur H is the more physically faithful listed proxy for the guaranteed sharp-vs-smeared shape distribution that separates curated GBIF photos from real transit captures. G remains the strongest alternative under the strict DOF calculation, with F as the only safe geometric invariance.

Unresolved: exact CoC/sensor size, true DOF extent, actual animal speed distribution in the pinch point, and whether defocus or motion dominates the loss of high-frequency cues in practise.

The deployment set is a fixed-geometry, fixed-photometry night IR trap and the training set is a free-form daylight RGB GBIF scrape. The dominant unclosed shift is modality: night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness IR illuminator, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s → essentially constant global brightness and R≈G≈B in the field. That makes linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C, RGB channel swizzle I, colour noise J and salt-and-pepper K mismatched; they inject variation never seen at test time and encourage reliance on daylight colour cues absent under IR. Scale D is essentially locked by the 7 m rock-to-rock baseline and the fixed ~50 mm optics. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-to-right vs right-to-left transit through the pinch point and is the only safe geometric invariance, a second-order data multiplier.

The remaining debate is optical quality vs capture dynamics.

G camp: f≈50 mm, N=4.0, focus s0≈3.5 m gives H≈f²/Nc≈20-31 m, near≈3.0 m, far≈4.0-4.2 m, i.e. ~1 m of acceptable focus in a 7 m channel. GBIF media is essentially all sharp in-focus daylight colour. In the field an animal is critically sharp only for a brief interval around the mid-plane; the majority of a transit is systematically defocused. 1/500 s =2 ms is argued to freeze in-plane translation to a few cm / a few pixels, so directional in-exposure motion blur H is second order to the always-present DOF loss. An isotropic 11×11 σ≈3 px Gaussian is the canonical proxy for that systematic depth-of-field defocus and forces EfficientNet-B7 features stable under loss of high-frequency edge cues. The true daylight RGB → fixed IR monochrome shift is not closed by any A-K; ideally grayscale/IR simulation and trap fine-tuning would be needed, i.e. L is strictly defensible. Of the listed ops G is the most deployment-relevant simulable effect, with F as the only safe geometric invariance.

H camp: the real train-test difference is static curated GBIF stills vs a live funnel trap sampling every 30 s with no trigger. Animals are transiting the corridor when the shutter fires, not posing. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of body width during ~2 ms and limbs/head/torso are at different gait phases in the same frame, producing spatially localised, directional smearing along the travel axis while the rock background stays sharp. A region-selective directional motion blur mimics that generation process and leaves the static background sharp as in the real rig. The DOF argument is fragile: the spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”, hyperfocal/DOF numbers depend critically on an unstated circle of confusion and sensor size, defocus is depth-varying and radial not a uniform whole-image Gaussian, and a global Gaussian blurs the rock faces/background texture that remain usable for localisation in the field and penalises use of cues that are in fact sharp in deployment. The pinch geometry also constrains lateral position and body depth ~0.3-0.6 m, so residence time outside the nominal ~1 m in-focus slab is short. Motion is guaranteed present in deployment and essentially absent from GBIF.

Unresolved tension persists. Current belief remains that among the listed operations the guaranteed hardware-imposed effect is systematic defocus, so G is the most deployment-relevant regulariser that can be simulated from the list, with horizontal mirroring F as a useful second-order invariance, while acknowledging the dominant colour→IR shift remains unmitigated by any listed augmentation and the motion-vs-defocus debate is still open.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we’re all converging on the same core problem, which the G camp has stated well: photometry/modality is essentially locked in deployment and geometry/scale is essentially locked. Fixed-brightness IR, night only, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s, R≈G≈B, 7 m standoff with ~50 mm optics focused at ~3.5 m. That really does make A,B,C,I,J,K and scale D and vertical flip E non-deployable, and it makes the daylight RGB GBIF → fixed IR monochrome shift the dominant, unclosed gap that none of A-K closes. Colleagues 10,11,12,6,8 are explicit about that, and it’s right.

Where I diverge is on which listed proxy is the most faithful physical mismatch that is guaranteed in the field and essentially absent from the GBIF scrape.

The hyperfocal numbers quoted for G are formally correct for an ideal lens, f≈50 mm N=4.0 s0≈3.5 m → H≈20-31 m, near≈3.0 m far≈4.0-4.2 m. The problem is how that maps to this rig in practice. First the spec itself is contradictory, “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”, and the near/far values hinge on an unstated circle of confusion and sensor format. Second defocus in a real lens is depth-varying and radial, not a uniform 11×11 σ=3 isotropic blur applied globally to the whole frame. A global Gaussian blurs the rock faces and the background texture that in deployment remain static and sharp and are actually a very reliable localisation cue for the network. It penalises the model for using cues that are present at test time.

The pinch point also changes how much an animal actually lives outside the nominal ~1 m in-focus slab. Travel is essentially along the optical axis and within a ~0.3-0.6 m body depth. Residence time in the extreme near/far zones is short relative to transit through the mid-plane, and the funnel forces the animal close to the optical axis. So the net time spent significantly defocused is modest, whereas the in-exposure sampling problem is present on every capture.

GBIF multimedia is curated daylight stills, mostly static/posed with crisp edges. The trap fires every 30 s with no trigger. The animal is sampled mid-transit. Even at 1/500 s = 2 ms a mammal moving a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of a body width during the exposure, and the gait cycle guarantees different parts of the body are at different phases within the same frame. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deployment rig is a highly constrained night-IR trap: camera bolted to rock face 7 m down a pinch point, nominal 50 mm effective focal length at f/4.0, ISO190, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illumination, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, one frame every 30 s, focused at ~3.5 m mid-point. Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species: daylight, visible colour, variable camera pose/distance, largely static sharp exemplars. 17 species.

Domain gaps therefore are:
* modality/photometry: deployment is essentially monochrome R≈G≈B under fixed illumination and locked exposure. Global brightness is essentially constant. Linear/non-linear brightness A,B,C, RGB swizzle I, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K are mismatched to test statistics and encourage reliance on colour/daylight cues absent at test time. No listed op creates a faithful IR/grayscale proxy.
* geometry/scale: 7 m standoff and narrow pinch point lock nominal object scale and viewpoint. Scale D is essentially irrelevant. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-right transit and is a safe geometric invariance but second order compared with image-quality effects.
* optics: f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m → hyperfocal ≈ f²/Nc ≈20-31 m, near≈ Hs/(H+s)≈3.0 m, far≈ Hs/(H-s)≈4.2 m, i.e. ~0.8-1.2 m DOF in a 7 m channel. Depth-of-field defocus is therefore a systematic, deployment-constant degradation for animals off the focus plane and is essentially absent from sharp GBIF media.
* dynamics: animals are funnelled through corridor and camera fires every 30 s with no trigger. Motion during 2 ms exposure, gait phase and transit direction create a small, spatially localised, directional smear on the animal while rock background stays sharp. GBIF is curated static natural-history photography.

Colleague split persists and has shifted slightly.
Defocus camp 11,12,2,3,4,6,8 argues the guaranteed hardware effect is defocus. 1/500 s freezes in-plane translation enough that motion blur H is small/secondary, and an isotropic Gaussian blur G is the canonical proxy for depth-of-field blur. Horizontal mirroring F is plausible but secondary. The colour→IR shift is not closed by any listed op; ideal fix would be grayscale/IR simulation / fine-tuning, so strictly L would be correct.

Motion camp 1,10,13,14,5,7,9 argues the train-test gap is capture dynamics not photometry. Brightness/scale/blur are locked, the real gap is static sharp GBIF vs moving night-IR transit. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s can smear a non-trivial fraction of body width/limb during exposure, directional and object-localised. A directional motion-blur kernel on animal regions mimics this; isotropic Gaussian G blurs rocks and background unphysically and overestimates defocus for animals constrained near the optical axis.

Additional notes from current round:
* Lens spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”, CoC unspecified, so DOF numbers are sensitive and the defocus argument is fragile.
* Motion proponents note a global isotropic Gaussian blurs the static rock faces that remain essentially sharp in deployment, whereas real defocus is depth-varying/radial and motion blur leaves background sharp.
* Defocus proponents note defocus is present for essentially every capture outside the narrow ~3.0-4.2 m slice and is independent of animal speed, whereas motion blur is speed dependent.
* Agreement across both camps: photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K are irrelevant / harmful; scale D irrelevant; vertical flip E harmful; colour/day → IR/monochrome shift is real and not closed by any listed augmentation. Horizontal flip F is the only safe geometric invariance.

Unresolved: magnitude of in-exposure translation vs depth-dependent defocus for animals confined to a pinch point slab; whether isotropic Gaussian is an adequate proxy for defocus vs a local directional motion blur; the exact CoC/sensor which determines DOF magnitude. Persistent belief: photometric augmentations are irrelevant, vertical flip harmful, scale irrelevant. The dominant unaddressed modality shift is colour/day → IR/monochrome, not present in A-K. Among listed ops the physically guaranteed simulable effect is depth-of-field defocus G, with H as a strong alternative interpretation of the dynamics gap, and F as the only safe geometric invariance.

* Modality shift daylight RGB GBIF → fixed-brightness IR monochrome night is the dominant unclosed gap. No listed operation faithfully creates grayscale/IR simulation; in a strict sense L “none of the above” is ideal. RGB swizzle I is the closest colour-invariance proxy but does not produce required monochrome IR statistics.

Competing image-quality mismatch arguments:

G camp: fixed focus at mid-point ~3.5 m, f≈50 mm, N=4.0 → H≈f²/Nc≈20–31 m, near≈3.0 m, far≈4.0–4.2 m, i.e. ~0.8–1.2 m of acceptable focus in a 7 m deep channel. H camp: spec contradiction “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length” and CoC/sensor unknown make DOF numbers fragile. Real defocus is depth-varying and radial, not a uniform whole-frame Gaussian. A global Gaussian blurs the static rock faces and background texture that in deployment remain sharp and usable for localisation, penalising cues that are present at test time. In a pinch point travel is largely along the optical axis within ~0.3–0.6 m body depth; residence time in extreme near/far zones is short and a substantial fraction of transit stays near the focus slab.

What is guaranteed and essentially absent from GBIF is capture dynamics: trap fires every 30 s with no trigger, animals are sampled mid-transit, not posed. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of a body width during the exposure and gait puts limbs/head/torso at different phases within the same frame. Motion is independent of CoC ambiguity and leaves background sharp as in the real rig.

Unresolved: actual sensor CoC/sensor format, true focal length, actual distribution of animal depth in the pinch point, actual speed distribution, and whether average defocus magnitude exceeds average in-exposure smear.

Current belief: dominant failure remains daylight colour → fixed IR monochrome, unaddressed by A-K. Of the listed candidates, the physically verifiable degradation that is guaranteed in deployment, absent from GBIF, and can be simulated without corrupting static background cues is directional, animal-localised motion blur. Gaussian defocus G is a strong alternative if DOF calculation is taken at face value, but it mis-models background sharpness and relies on fragile optics assumptions. Horizontal flip F is the only safe geometric invariance. Photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K, scale D, vertical flip E, generic Gaussian G applied globally, and salt-and-pepper K are mismatched or harmful.

reflection_text.4:
The deployment rig is a highly constrained night-IR trap: camera bolted to rock face 7 m down a pinch point, nominal 50 mm effective focal length at f/4.0, ISO190, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illumination, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, one frame every 30 s, focused at ~3.5 m mid-point. Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species: daylight, visible colour, variable camera pose/distance, largely static sharp exemplars. 17 species.

Domain gaps therefore are:
* modality/photometry: deployment is essentially monochrome R≈G≈B under fixed illumination and locked exposure. Global brightness is essentially constant. Linear/non-linear brightness A,B,C, RGB swizzle I, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K are mismatched to test statistics and encourage reliance on colour/daylight cues absent at test time. No listed op creates a faithful IR/grayscale proxy.
* geometry/scale: 7 m standoff and narrow pinch point lock nominal object scale and viewpoint. Scale D is essentially irrelevant. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-right transit and is a safe geometric invariance but second order compared with image-quality effects.
* optics: f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m → hyperfocal ≈ f²/Nc ≈20-31 m, near≈ Hs/(H+s)≈3.0 m, far≈ Hs/(H-s)≈4.2 m, i.e. ~0.8-1.2 m DOF in a 7 m channel. Depth-of-field defocus is therefore a systematic, deployment-constant degradation for animals off the focus plane and is essentially absent from sharp GBIF media.
* dynamics: animals are funnelled through corridor and camera fires every 30 s with no trigger. Motion during 2 ms exposure, gait phase and transit direction create a small, spatially localised, directional smear on the animal while rock background stays sharp. GBIF is curated static natural-history photography.

Colleague split persists and has shifted slightly.
Defocus camp 11,12,2,3,4,6,8 argues the guaranteed hardware effect is defocus. 1/500 s freezes in-plane translation enough that motion blur H is small/secondary, and an isotropic Gaussian blur G is the canonical proxy for depth-of-field blur. Horizontal mirroring F is plausible but secondary. The colour→IR shift is not closed by any listed op; ideal fix would be grayscale/IR simulation / fine-tuning, so strictly L would be correct.

Motion camp 1,10,13,14,5,7,9 argues the train-test gap is capture dynamics not photometry. Brightness/scale/blur are locked, the real gap is static sharp GBIF vs moving night-IR transit. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s can smear a non-trivial fraction of body width/limb during exposure, directional and object-localised. A directional motion-blur kernel on animal regions mimics this; isotropic Gaussian G blurs rocks and background unphysically and overestimates defocus for animals constrained near the optical axis.

Additional notes from current round:
* Lens spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”, CoC unspecified, so DOF numbers are sensitive and the defocus argument is fragile.
* Motion proponents note a global isotropic Gaussian blurs the static rock faces that remain essentially sharp in deployment, whereas real defocus is depth-varying/radial and motion blur leaves background sharp.
* Defocus proponents note defocus is present for essentially every capture outside the narrow ~3.0-4.2 m slice and is independent of animal speed, whereas motion blur is speed dependent.
* Agreement across both camps: photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K are irrelevant / harmful; scale D irrelevant; vertical flip E harmful; colour/day → IR/monochrome shift is real and not closed by any listed augmentation. Horizontal flip F is the only safe geometric invariance.

Unresolved: magnitude of in-exposure translation vs depth-dependent defocus for animals confined to a pinch point slab; whether isotropic Gaussian is an adequate proxy for defocus vs a local directional motion blur; the exact CoC/sensor which determines DOF magnitude. Persistent belief: photometric augmentations are irrelevant, vertical flip harmful, scale irrelevant. The dominant unaddressed modality shift is colour/day → IR/monochrome, not present in A-K. Among listed ops the physically guaranteed simulable effect is depth-of-field defocus G, with H as a strong alternative interpretation of the dynamics gap, and F as the only safe geometric invariance.
reflection_text.3:
The train-test gap is fixed IR camera-trap rig vs broad GBIF colour daylight scrape, not generic ImageNet.

Deployment physics that are stable and now repeatedly affirmed:
* Fixed photometry/modality: rock face to rock face 7 m, ~50 mm optics, f/4.0, ISO 190, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illumination, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, one frame every 30 s. Brightness/exposure essentially constant and R≈G≈B under IR. Linear/non-linear brightness A,B,C, RGB swizzle I, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K inject variation that will never be seen at test time and encourage reliance on daylight colour cues absent under fixed IR.
* Geometry/scale essentially locked by 7 m pinch point and fixed optics. Scale D is of little value. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically realisable left-to-right vs right-to-left transit and is a safe second-order geometric invariance.
* Modality shift daylight RGB GBIF → fixed-brightness IR monochrome night is the dominant unclosed gap. No listed operation faithfully creates grayscale/IR simulation; in a strict sense L “none of the above” is ideal. RGB swizzle I is the closest colour-invariance proxy but does not produce required monochrome IR statistics.

Competing image-quality mismatch arguments:

G camp: fixed focus at mid-point ~3.5 m, f≈50 mm, N=4.0 → H≈f²/Nc≈20–31 m, near≈3.0 m, far≈4.0–4.2 m, i.e. ~0.8–1.2 m of acceptable focus in a 7 m deep channel. GBIF is essentially all sharp, in-focus daylight. Depth-of-field defocus is guaranteed by focus/aperture geometry and is systematically absent from training. An 11×11 σ≈3 px isotropic Gaussian is the canonical proxy for that systematic loss of high-frequency edge detail. Motion blur H is small at 1/500 s =2 ms for mostly axial transit, so directional in-exposure motion is second order to always-present optical defocus.

H camp: spec contradiction “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length” and CoC/sensor unknown make DOF numbers fragile. Real defocus is depth-varying and radial, not a uniform whole-frame Gaussian. A global Gaussian blurs the static rock faces and background texture that in deployment remain sharp and usable for localisation, penalising cues that are present at test time. In a pinch point travel is largely along the optical axis within ~0.3–0.6 m body depth; residence time in extreme near/far zones is short and a substantial fraction of transit stays near the focus slab.

What is guaranteed and essentially absent from GBIF is capture dynamics: trap fires every 30 s with no trigger, animals are sampled mid-transit, not posed. Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of a body width during the exposure and gait puts limbs/head/torso at different phases within the same frame. That produces spatially localised, directional smearing along corridor axis while rocks stay crisp. Region-selective directional motion blur reproduces that generation process and forces EfficientNet-B7 to keep shape/texture invariants that survive a small streak rather than over-relying on pristine high-frequency edges dominant in GBIF. Motion is independent of CoC ambiguity and leaves background sharp as in the real rig.

Unresolved: actual sensor CoC/sensor format, true focal length, actual distribution of animal depth in the pinch point, actual speed distribution, and whether average defocus magnitude exceeds average in-exposure smear.

Current belief: dominant failure remains daylight colour → fixed IR monochrome, unaddressed by A-K. Of the listed candidates, the physically verifiable degradation that is guaranteed in deployment, absent from GBIF, and can be simulated without corrupting static background cues is directional, animal-localised motion blur. Gaussian defocus G is a strong alternative if DOF calculation is taken at face value, but it mis-models background sharpness and relies on fragile optics assumptions. Horizontal flip F is the only safe geometric invariance. Photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K, scale D, vertical flip E, generic Gaussian G applied globally, and salt-and-pepper K are mismatched or harmful.

The dominant unclosed failure is daylight RGB → fixed IR monochrome. No listed op closes it; ideal is grayscale/IR simulation + trap fine-tuning, i.e. L in strict sense. Colleagues 10,4,12,1,8 agree.

Geometry / scale lock:
Camera bolted 7 m down a pinch point, ~50 mm optics, focus at ~3.5 m mid-plane. Apparent size is quasi-constant, so scale D is of little value. Vertical flip E is physically impossible for terrestrial mammals. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible left-to-right vs right-to-left transit and is the only safe geometric invariance; colleagues 12,3,5,8 note it is second order vs optical/dynamic degradation.

Optics vs motion tension remains the core disagreement.

DOF / G camp:
f≈50 mm, N=4.0, s0≈3.5 m → hyperfocal ≈20–31 m, near≈3.0 m, far≈4.0–4.2 m → ~1 m of acceptable focus in a 7 m corridor. GBIF set is essentially all sharp daylight colour. Isotropic Gaussian blur is the canonical proxy for systematic depth-of-field defocus. 1/500 s freezes in-plane translation for mostly axial transit, so motion blur H is second order. Colleagues 11,12,2,3,4,6,8 argue G is the most deployment-relevant regulariser that can be simulated from the list, with F as only safe geometric gain.

Motion / H camp:
Spec is contradictory “105 mm wide angle lens with a 50 mm focal length”; DOF numbers are CoC/sensor-sensitive and unstated. Real defocus is depth-varying and radial, not a uniform 11×11 σ=3 blur applied globally to the whole frame. A global Gaussian blurs rock faces and background texture that in deployment remain sharp and are a stable reference, and blurs background and foreground identically, which is not how a fixed-focus lens behaves. Pinch geometry constrains depth; travel is essentially along optical axis within ~0.3–0.6 m body depth, residence time in extreme near/far zones is short. 1/500 s =2 ms still samples mid-gait; a mammal moving a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of body width during exposure and limbs/head/torso are at different phases. That produces spatially localised, directional smearing along travel axis while static rocks stay crisp. Region-selective directional motion blur replicates that generation process and forces EfficientNet-B7 to keep shape/texture invariants that survive a small streak, rather than over-relying on pristine high-frequency edges in GBIF. Colleagues 1,10,13,14,7,5,9 make this case; they also note H is guaranteed and independent of CoC ambiguity.

Current synthesis:
Colour/brightness/noise/scale/vertical flip augmentations are mismatched to fixed IR, fixed exposure, fixed-range rig. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible but second order.
The real unaddressed failure is daylight colour → fixed IR monochrome, unclosed by any listed op.
Among simulable degradations, the disagreement is systematic depth-of-field defocus vs in-exposure transit motion.
The uniform Gaussian G argument rests on a guaranteed depth-of-field loss for most of the 7 m corridor. The motion H argument rests on physical fidelity – region-selective directional smear with a sharp static background, and the critique that a global isotropic Gaussian mis-models both depth-varying defocus and the sharp rock reference, plus lens spec contradiction and CoC sensitivity.
Given the repeated critique of global isotropic blur blurring the static reference background and the contradictory lens spec / CoC sensitivity, motion blur H is the more physically faithful listed proxy for the guaranteed sharp-vs-smeared shape distribution that separates curated GBIF photos from real transit captures. G remains the strongest alternative under strict DOF calculation, with F as the only safe geometric invariance.

Unresolved: exact CoC/sensor size, true DOF extent with the contradictory 105 mm / 50 mm spec, actual animal speed distribution in the pinch point, proportion of transit time spent outside the nominal ~3–4.2 m focus slab vs in-exposure motion magnitude, and whether defocus or motion dominates loss of high-frequency cues in practice.

Ideal fix would be grayscale/IR simulation + trap fine-tuning, supporting a strict None L argument. Several colleagues explicitly state this.

Live disagreement is defocus vs motion.

Defocus / Gaussian blur G camp:

Motion blur H camp:
* Train-test mismatch is dynamic, not photometric. GBIF multimedia is curated static daylight natural history. Deployment fires every 30 s with no trigger in a funnel; animals are transiting when shutter opens.
* Even at 1/500 s a mammal moving a few m/s moves a non-trivial fraction of body width during ~2 ms exposure; gait cycle gives different phases within frame. Blur is directional, spatially localised to animal, rock background stays sharp.

* Scale D essentially fixed by 7 m standoff and fixed optics.

Current best working hypothesis remains split: among strictly listed options the physically grounded effect guaranteed by stated focus/f-number/geometry is systematic defocus, best approximated by Gaussian blur G; motion blur H is a credible alternative with strong arguments about background sharpness, spec contradiction, and dominance of transit dynamics over depth variation.
